passage:
A handwritten book was not made page by page. Sheets of parchment were folded once down the middle, laid inside one another in a small stack, and sewn through the fold. The stack, most often four sheets and so sixteen sides to write on, was the unit in which a scribe worked, and it is called a gathering. A volume was assembled out of gatherings only after each of them had been finished separately.

The arrangement has a consequence that the finished page hides. Folding a sheet produces two leaves that are joined to each other through the fold but are not adjacent in the book: a leaf near the front of a gathering is one piece of parchment with a leaf near the back. Cut one of the pair away and the other, though nothing has been done to it, has nothing left to hold it in place. It works loose, and in a great many surviving volumes it has been lost in its turn, at a point far from the original damage.

What the cutting leaves behind is a narrow ridge of parchment at the fold, called a stub. The stub is a fact about the object and not about the text, and the two need not agree: the sentences on either side of a missing leaf can run on smoothly enough that a reader following the sense notices nothing. The scribes left a second mark that helps here. At the foot of the last page of a gathering the scribe copied the first word of the next gathering, a catchword, so that the finished stacks could be put in order; a catchword that answers to nothing is a gathering that has gone.

Not every departure from the expected pattern is damage. A scribe who came to the end of a text with more parchment in hand than the work needed, or with less, altered the last gathering to suit, and final gatherings of three sheets or of five are common in volumes that have lost nothing at all. The structure has to be read sheet by sheet before it can be interpreted, and a count of leaves will not do it.
prompt: [Academic — Codicology] What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The physical construction of a manuscript preserves evidence about its making and its losses that the text does not reveal.
Most of what a manuscript has lost can be recovered by comparing it with other surviving copies of the same text.
The losses a manuscript has suffered can usually be dated from the way its gatherings were sewn and afterwards repaired.
Scribes built gatherings so that damage to one leaf of a book would not affect the leaves lying around it.
correct_answer: The physical construction of a manuscript preserves evidence about its making and its losses that the text does not reveal.
explanation: Each paragraph reads the object rather than the writing: the second derives a loss the page hides, the third sets the stub and the catchword against sentences that "run on smoothly", and the fourth warns that "a count of leaves will not do it" — that is the statement about construction preserving evidence the text does not reveal. No paragraph mentions other surviving copies of the text, still less recovering losses by comparing them. Nothing in the passage dates losses from the sewing or from a later repair. And the second paragraph says the opposite of leaves lying around each other undamaged: cutting one leaf is what loosens its partner.

choices: work loose from the volume although nothing has been done to it.
sit immediately beside the gap that the cutting has opened in the text.
leave behind it the narrow ridge of parchment called a stub.
be sewn back into its own gathering by a binder at some later date of repair.

prompt: [Academic — Codicology] Why does the author state that a volume was assembled out of gatherings only after each of them had been finished?
choices: To explain why the two leaves of one sheet remain joined to each other through the fold.
To suggest that several scribes could be at work on a single volume at the same time.
To establish that the scribe's unit of work was the stack of folded sheets and not the finished book.
To show that a volume could be bound by someone who had never read the text it carried.
correct_answer: To establish that the scribe's unit of work was the stack of folded sheets and not the finished book.
explanation: The first paragraph builds to the claim that the stack was "the unit in which a scribe worked", and the remark about assembly is what makes the point: the book came together only afterwards. The joining of two leaves through the fold is a result of folding, introduced in the next paragraph, not of the order of assembly. Nothing in the passage puts more than one scribe on a volume, and nothing is said about whether a binder could read.

choices: was left unfinished by a scribe who stopped copying before the end of the text had been reached.
may be complete, since a scribe could alter the last gathering to fit the text that was left.
may have lost a pair of joined leaves from somewhere near the middle of that final gathering.
was copied from an exemplar that ended at a different point in the text from the one planned for.
correct_answer: may be complete, since a scribe could alter the last gathering to fit the text that was left.

The passage never describes a scribe abandoning a text partway, and it says nothing about the exemplar a scribe copied from.

passage:
Before a scribe wrote anything, the page was prepared to receive the writing. A row of small holes, the prickings, was pierced down the margins of a folded stack of sheets, and a line was then drawn across the sheet from each hole to the hole facing it. The result was a grid: horizontal lines to carry the writing, and two or more vertical lines fixing where each line of text would begin and where it would stop. Ink came last.

Because the holes were pierced through the whole stack at once, the grid repeats through every sheet of the gathering, the stack of folded sheets sewn together as a single unit, and the pattern on the outermost sheet answers to the pattern on the innermost. A volume in which that pattern changes partway through, with a different number of written lines to the page, a wider inner margin, or prickings that stop and resume in a slightly different rhythm, was made in more than one campaign, whatever the uniformity of the hand may suggest. A script can be imitated, and often was. A ruling grid is workshop equipment, and there is nothing to be had by imitating it.

How closely a scribe obeyed the grid varies, and the variation is informative. In a plain prose text the writing generally sits on the ruled line without incident. In verse, in tables, and in commentary crowded around a central text, a scribe who has misjudged the space will run past the vertical bounding line, perch a last word above it, or force two lines of writing into a single ruled space. Each such lapse marks a place where the text and the plan made for it disagreed.

Ruling styles changed slowly and differed from region to region, so a grid can be given a place and an approximate date. What it dates, though, is the preparation of the parchment. Prepared sheets were stored, and they were traded; a scribe in one town could write on a grid ruled some years earlier in another. Grid and handwriting answer different questions, and a study that treats them as one has assumed what it ought to be showing.
prompt: [Academic — Codicology] According to the passage, the row of holes pierced down the margins was used to
choices: show the scribe how many sheets the stack in hand contained.
mark the points at which the sheets would afterwards be sewn.
divide each sheet into the two leaves that a single fold produces.
place the horizontal lines that the writing would later sit on.
correct_answer: place the horizontal lines that the writing would later sit on.
explanation: The first paragraph draws a line "from each hole to the hole facing it" and calls the result horizontal lines "to carry the writing", which is the option about placing the lines the writing would sit on. The sewing, the count of sheets in the stack and the folding into leaves are all mentioned elsewhere in the passage but never as work the prickings do.

choices: To show that the grid was drawn for the convenience of the binder rather than the reader.
To indicate that the ruling was carried out by craftsmen rather than by the scribe himself.
To suggest that one grid was prepared once and then reused for a great many texts.

correct_answer: To explain why no one would trouble to copy a grid the way a hand could be copied.
